content: Cefadroxil, a first-generation cephalosporin antibiotic, is used to treat a variety of bacterial infections by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis, thereby arresting bacterial growth. It is effective against rapidly growing organisms and is primarily excreted unchanged in the urine (90%). Its metabolism in the liver is minimal, and it has a volume of distribution of approximately 31 L/kg. This medication is generally considered safe during pregnancy (Category B) and enters breast milk, so caution is advised during lactation. Drug Interactions: 1. Hormonal Contraceptives: Cefadroxil may reduce the effectiveness of oral hormonal contraceptives (e.g., conjugated estrogens, ethinyl estradiol, levonorgestrel) by altering intestinal flora. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and monitoring are recommended. 2. Acidic Drugs: Cefadroxil can increase the levels or effects of acidic drugs (e.g., etodolac, fenbufen, ibuprofen, indomethacin, ketoprofen, meloxicam, naproxen) by competing for renal tubular clearance. These interactions are generally minor, with unknown clinical significance. 3. Nephrotoxic Agents: Cefadroxil may increase the nephrotoxic effects of aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin, kanamycin, tobramycin, streptomycin) and other nephrotoxic drugs (e.g., voclosporin). This can elevate the risk of acute or chronic kidney toxicity. Close monitoring and caution are advised. 4. Live Vaccines: Cefadroxil can reduce the efficacy of live bacterial vaccines (e.g., typhoid vaccine) due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live vaccines should be administered only after completing the antibiotic course. 5. Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors: Cefadroxil may interfere with the therapeutic effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., nivolumab, pembrolizumab, toripalimab) through unspecified mechanisms. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 6. Other Interactions: Cefadroxil may alter the levels or effects of various drugs, including diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, furosemide), antivirals (e.g., ganciclovir, valganciclovir), and anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin). It may also reduce the efficacy of certain vitamins (e.g., thiamine, pyridoxine) by altering intestinal flora. Side Effects: Common side effects include gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. Rare but serious adverse effects include pseudomembranous colitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, anaphylaxis, and increased liver enzymes. Prolonged use may lead to superinfections, such as oral thrush or yeast infections. Precautions: Allergies: Inform your doctor if you are allergic to cefadroxil, penicillins, or other cephalosporins. Diabetes: The liquid suspension may contain sugar, so caution is advised for patients with diabetes. Renal Impairment: Dosage adjustments are necessary in severe renal insufficiency to prevent central nervous system toxicity. Pregnancy and Lactation: Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Exercise caution while breastfeeding. Administration: Cefadroxil is taken orally, with or without food, usually once or twice daily as directed by your doctor. Complete the full prescribed course, even if symptoms improve, to prevent the development of antibiotic resistance. Storage: Store capsules and tablets at room temperature, away from light and moisture. The liquid suspension should be refrigerated and discarded after 14 days. Do not freeze the suspension. Overdose: In case of overdose, seek immediate medical attention. Symptoms may include severe gastrointestinal distress or central nervous system effects. Contact a poison control center for guidance. Important Notes: This summary does not include all possible information about cefadroxil. Always consult your healthcare provider for personalized medical advice and complete information about this medication.
